participants.name: baseline-array
participants.docs: no library — a Map plus a full rescan per settle
participants.admission: no library, and it is not a library claim: the harness owns the Map the values live in and the dirty flag that drives the consumer. This is the naive hand-written arm, and the ANCHOR only for the scenarios `baseline-indexed` declines.
participants.departure: no library and no documented recipe: this participant is the naive hand-written floor, the anchor only where `baseline-indexed` declines, and three things it does are its own. On the wide mount shape the subscriber joins the callback list of every churn row it is asked for and its body reads the first of them alone. On the chain shape it BUILDS NO DERIVATION: there is nothing here to stack, so the mount is the same per-row lists the wide shape makes and the body reads every root once and then applies every level of the depth on each wake; on the diamond shape the body computes both sides and the join itself, guarded by a settle counter so it runs at most once per settle. And every settle probes the `label` column list of each row written, one Map read, which the row-shaped churn scripts never populate.

participants.name: baseline-indexed
participants.docs: no library — a Map, a per-group bucket, and a re-derive per settle of each bucket whose window a write can change
participants.admission: no library, and it is not a library claim: the harness owns the Map, the buckets and the change signal. It is the ANCHOR every ratio is divided by wherever it takes part — the competent hand-written arm — and its gap to `baseline-array` is the price of a group index plus the re-renders it skips for writes nothing on screen depends on.
participants.departure: no library and no documented recipe: this row's storage model is the suite's own invention — a row bucket per group, kept up to date on write, ORDER MAINTAINED NOWHERE: a render selects its window out of the bucket with the same top-k the other anchor runs over the population. A point write marks a bucket only when its window can change — a note write never (no window renders it), a label write only for an entity on screen, a rank or group write only for an entity on screen or entering it — and a settle re-derives those buckets alone; the read binding marks view A and view B separately (a scroll or a switch marks A alone). A bucket is left in O(1) by swapping its last row into the vacated position. Nothing here is cited from anywhere.

participants.name: oimdb
participants.docs: packages/core/dist (the built package, as a consumer gets it) — createOIMEntityService(db, …) on one OIMDB with the default entity writer, createOIMEntityWriterInPlace(), and one createStoreSlot(db) as the instance; a first load goes in through entityService.slotContentService.insertEntities(entityStoreSlot, …), later writes through slotContentService.upsertEntities; a label or note patch assigns slot.entity in place and calls slotContentService.markEntityChanged with that one column, a group or rank move is slotContentService.updateEntityColumn on the slot entityService.getSlotByKey returns; a createOIMIndexService with an OIMSlotContentBucketServiceSetDriven over the group column, with indexService.createIndexStoreSlot(entityStoreSlot) as its instance, files each write into its buckets from keyOf, and a createOIMComputedServiceSorted over that index service (rank then id, as sortColumns, so only a write that changes rank or id on a member re-sorts), read through createSortedStoreSlot(indexStoreSlot), keeps the order of a held group as a computed slot; the read views wake on that order too, one per index; the churn chain levels are slots of one createOIMComputedService store slot and the diamond nodes slots of another, each keyed by subscriber and level, under one OIMEffectService.INSTANCE.createEffect(db, …) on the head; a frame of the window and read bindings is one OIMChannelService.INSTANCE.openSubframe/closeSubframe subframe on db.defaultChannelSlot
participants.admission: the row values live in the library — an entity service's slots, written through its slotContentService's insertEntities, upsertEntities, updateEntityColumn and markEntityChanged, and read back as slot.entity — and the change signal is the library's own OIMEffectService effect over a slot, a column, a bucket or an index order, delivered at the frame flush; the GROUP FILING and the ORDER are the library's too, an OIMIndexService whose entity service calls keyOf on each write, moves the row between its buckets itself and an OIMComputedServiceSorted re-sorts a held group's order when a write touches the sorter's columns.
participants.departure: measured against source that is not released: @oimdb/core 4.0.0 is unpublished and imported from the working tree. Two things it does that no other row pays for or is credited with: an index bucket is minted only when a key is held, so the two-view bindings file into the two groups a view watches and into no other, where several rows here keep a bucket per group whether or not anybody watches it — the fifty-view binding holds all fifty and files into all fifty; and on the wide mount shape the subscriber is registered over every churn row it is asked for while its body reads the first of them alone. Every binding with entity collections tears down with one OIMChannelService.INSTANCE.dropChannelSlot(db.defaultChannelSlot) and clears its own arrays: no effect is detached and no hold given back one at a time, because a dropped channel neither schedules nor runs a frame, so no effect body runs again. The single binding disposes its two effects and keeps its channel.

participants.name: oimdb-sorted-index
participants.docs: packages/core/dist (the built package, as a consumer gets it) — the same wiring as the oimdb row except for group order: a createOIMIndexServiceSortedArrayDriven over the group column with sortColumns rank then id, and indexService.createIndexStoreSlot(entityStoreSlot) as its instance, files each write into its buckets from keyOf and keeps every bucket in that order at the write, so there is no createOIMComputedServiceSorted; a window or read view reads its page with indexService.slotContentService.getBucketMemberSlotCount and getBucketMemberSlotAt from its offset, and its order effect has the held bucket slot as a root slot, which the index writes when membership changes or a member's rank or id changes; the read binding builds two such indexes, the group and the second axis

participants.name: oimdb-3.12.1
participants.admission: the row columns live in the entity slots of a 3.12.1 collection and are grouped and ordered by its own derived array index; the change signal is the engine's keyed emitters — collection.emitter per row and index.emitter per bucket — delivered at the event queue's frame end.
participants.departure: subscribed through collection.emitter and index.emitter, which the 3.x README never mentions: the updateEventEmitter.subscribeOnKey its examples use does not exist in 3.12.1's source, so the recipe here is the source rather than the shipped documentation. The churn binding alone builds its collection as `new OIMReactiveCollection` instead of through createOIMCollectionKit, because the kit's options type has no createUpdateEmitter and the column shape subscribes through OIMCarrierKeyedFieldEmitter.subscribeOnKeyFields. Its chain and diamond shapes build OIMComputed and OIMEffect on the queue's getOIMComputeRuntime instead of kit.computed and kit.effect, because the kit's dispose scope has no removal and an unmounted derivation would stay registered in it until the kit is destroyed.

participants.name: tinybase
participants.admission: the row values live in a TinyBase Store's cells and the change signal is the library's own — addResultSortedRowIdsListener and addResultRowListener on a query, addResultCellListener on the head of a chain of queries and on the join of a diamond, addCellListener on a cell — all called by TinyBase when the transaction finishes; the adapter keeps no values of its own.
participants.departure: a sorted result sorts on ONE cell, so each view query selects a calculated cell joining a fixed-width rank to the row id and TinyBase sorts and windows on that; the read and churn wirings also store the row id as a cell, because a where callback is handed no row id and the second axis and the chain's root rows are both predicates on it. Each chain subscriber builds its own root query, which TinyBase evaluates over the whole table at mount, and each diamond subscriber builds two such root queries and a third rooted on the left result that joins the right one by row id. A view switch re-runs the paged query's definition through setParamValue. On the wide shape it registers a row listener per churn row it is asked for and each body reads the first of them alone.

participants.name: signaldb
participants.admission: the row values live in a SignalDB Collection's documents and the change signal is the library's own cursor observeChanges, fired from the collection's write inside Observer.runChecks; the adapter-side `written` Set holds ids only, to choose insert over updateOne, and no row value is in it.
participants.departure: run with NO reactivity adapter installed — SignalDB takes its reactivity from Angular, Vue or Solid in every documented example, and installing one would measure that framework — so observeChanges drives the consumer instead; and the documented updateOne({ upsert: true }) is split into insert/updateOne on an adapter-side id Set, because its absent-row path copies and scans the whole collection twice. A frame is one collection.batch, opened once per frame because batch does not nest. On the wide mount shape one $in cursor observes every churn row it is asked for and its body keeps the first one's label out of the rows added and changed carry. The chain and diamond shapes bridge a cursor's observeChanges into @preact/signals-core signals and derive through its computed, since SignalDB exports no computed and no reactivity adapter is installed. A scroll or a view switch builds a new cursor, since a cursor takes its selector and skip at construction.

participants.name: tanstack-db
participants.admission: the row values live in a TanStack DB collection, written through its own sync interface (begin/write/commit), and the change signal is the library's own subscribeChanges on a live query collection, fired from commit() before the write returns; the adapter keeps no values of its own.
participants.departure: WRITES DO NOT GO THROUGH collection.insert/update/delete, the API an application calls: they are pushed through the sync handles (begin/write/commit) a collection-options creator gets, so the optimistic mutation path (transactions, optimistic state, rollback) is never entered and no figure here prices it; that path settles on a microtask and this harness never yields. A frame is one sync transaction per collection (begin … commit), and a write outside a frame is its own begin/write/commit. The diamond join is a live query over the two branch live queries; in 0.15 a committed batch is published in one scheduling context with the branches as its dependencies, and churnDiamond verifies it runs once per write. A view switch builds a new live query, since a where is fixed at construction; so does a scroll on the unindexed row, whose setWindow would return a promise. On the wide mount shape one subscription filters on every churn row it is asked for and its body reads the first of them alone. autoIndex is left at its default, off, which the library warns about once per ordered live query; the warning's two remedies are an explicit createIndex on rank (tanstack-db-indexed) and autoIndex: eager (tanstack-db-eager).

participants.name: tanstack-db-eager
participants.admission: the row values live in a TanStack DB collection, written through its own sync interface (begin/write/commit) and indexed by the library under autoIndex: eager, and the change signal is its own subscribeChanges on a live query collection, fired from commit() before the write returns; the adapter keeps no values of its own.

Eager also indexes the where of every subscribeChanges, so the churn and single wirings build an index on id that no script reads (no subscription asks for initial state), and on churn that build lands in the first timed mount of the process.

participants.name: tanstack-db-indexed
participants.admission: the row values live in a TanStack DB collection, written through its own sync interface (begin/write/commit) and indexed by collection.createIndex, and the change signal is the library's own subscribeChanges on a live query collection, fired from commit() before the write returns; the adapter keeps no values of its own.
participants.departure: WRITES DO NOT GO THROUGH collection.insert/update/delete, the API an application calls: they are pushed through the sync handles (begin/write/commit) a collection-options creator gets, so the optimistic mutation path (transactions, optimistic state, rollback) is never entered and no figure here prices it; that path settles on a microtask and this harness never yields. participants.name: lokijs
participants.admission: the row columns live in LokiJS documents inside its own collection, which is also what groups and orders them, and the change signal is the collection emitter firing insert, update and delete synchronously on every write.
participants.departure: Loki's own view signal on a passive view is a throttled setTimeout 'rebuild', which never fires in a harness that never yields; settle therefore calls each DynamicView's performSortPhase(), which emits 'rebuild' synchronously only for a view LokiJS dirtied, so which views render is still LokiJS's decision, but a settle per step turns a design that coalesces on purpose into a view re-sort per step. LokiJS has no notification batch (its collection transaction is a rollback snapshot), so a frame runs its writes directly. No binary index is built, though the cited indexing guide recommends one. On the churn rows the collection emitter means there is NO PER-SOURCE subscription: every subscriber runs on every write and tests the document for itself. The column, chain and diamond shapes are declined. A view switch replaces the paged DynamicView's group filter by its uid (applyFind), which re-runs that view over the whole collection.

participants.name: mobx
participants.admission: every mutable column lives in its own MobX atom, on class instances annotated with makeObservable (MobX's documented store shape: accessors on the instance, no Proxy) held in an observable.map, and the group index is an observable.map of observable.sets of those same objects rather than of values; the change signal is MobX's own autorun over a computed, run at the end of the outermost action, and the chain, the diamond and the view switch are computeds and observable.boxes MobX re-evaluates itself.
participants.departure: its row-shaped churn subscriber reads all four of a row's atoms rather than the one column the churn line renders — MobX tracks per PROPERTY, so a subscriber that read one would be the column shape under another name, while the chain and diamond derive from the label alone as every adapter's do; a removal leaves the group index through one observable.set delete per id, where other rows splice or rebuild the group's array; and the timed teardown disposes the reactions only, leaving the observable map the population lives in to the collector.

participants.name: jotai
participants.admission: every row lives in its own jotai atom, one per key via `jotai-family`, read and written through the store — and each consumer is driven by `store.sub` on a derived view atom that reads per-column derived atoms (group, rank, label) and selects ids, flushed inside the write, its listener reading the selected rows back through `store.get`. The per-group ids atoms hold keys only, never a value, and the population audit enumerates the family's own `getParams` rather than any list this adapter keeps.
participants.departure: a removal rebuilds each touched group's ids atom once for the whole batch rather than per removed row; and the timed teardown unsubscribes the view atoms only, leaving the store and its atom families to the collector.

participants.name: legend-state
participants.admission: every column lives in a Legend-State `observable` keyed by id, written through the node and read back with `get()`/`peek()` — and each consumer is driven by `observe`, re-run from the library's own notification pass. The second observable this adapter keeps maps each group to an object keyed by member id (`byGroup[group][id].set(true)` / `.delete()`), never a value.
participants.departure: the timed teardown disposes the standing reactions only, leaving the observables the population lives in to the collector.

participants.name: effector
participants.admission: the rows live in Effector `Store`s — one per group in the window wiring, beside an id -> group-store table that holds handles only; one holding a Map keyed by id in the read wiring, whose `byGroup` index holds ids only, never a value; one per row in the churn and relation wirings — replaced by a reducer on every write, and each consumer is driven by `.watch` or `.updates.watch` on the store it reads.
participants.departure: a reducer must be pure, so a point write copies the Map of the store it lands in, where the other rows assign into the row they already hold. The window and cell wirings hold one store PER GROUP, created at bind for the watched groups because a derived store fixes its inputs at construction, so a point write copies its own group's Map, wakes that group's view alone, and a move is two events on two stores. Effector 23 exports no batch(fn), so in those two wirings `frame` collects the frame's writes and fires ONE event per touched group store with the array of them, the Effector idiom for a bulk edit: the store copies its Map once and its view recomputes once per frame. Each pinned cell is a `.map` of its row's group store down to one column's string, so Effector's own `===` skip keeps a label write away from the note consumer. The read wiring keeps the population in ONE store, because view A re-points to another group on a switch and a `combine` cannot change its inputs, so a point write there copies all of it; only the four moves of the two-axis script write there. In the churn, read, relation and single wirings `frame` calls its function directly. The churn wiring, which subscribes only after `holdChurnRows` has resolved its rows, holds a `Store` per row and copies that row alone, as the relation wiring does for its owners. The window array a derived store produces is allocated fresh on every recomputation, so Effector's own identity skip can never fire on a view; and a removal rebuilds each touched store once for the whole batch rather than per removed row.

participants.name: nanostores
participants.admission: the row columns live in the records of nanostores map stores — one per group in the window wiring, beside an id -> store table that holds handles only, and one for the population in the read wiring, beside a group index that holds ids alone and no value; the change signal is the store's own notify — inline outside a frame, drained once at the end of `batch` inside one — reaching the consumer through the subscribed computed built over it.
participants.departure: `frame` is the library's own synchronous `batch(fn)` (atom/index.js:43-57), which queues every listener and drains once when the outermost batch returns, so a frame of writes notifies each listener once. The load and every batched write are published as ONE whole-record map.set per touched store rather than the documented per-key setKey: setKey copies the whole record on every call, so per-key writes would make one call to write into ten thousand record copies, batched or not. THE POINT WRITES PAY A RECORD COPY, and nothing in the library avoids it: setKey is `{ ...value, [key]: value }` (map/index.js) and deepMap's setPath copies the top level as well (deep-map/path.js). The window and cell wirings hold one map store PER GROUP, created at bind for the watched groups because computed fixes its dependency list at construction, so a point write spreads its own group's record and a move writes two stores. Each pinned cell is a computed over its row's group store down to one column's string, and each column a computed over its cells, so the atom's own Object.is keeps a label write away from the note consumer. The read wiring, whose two views are both over one group, keeps the population in ONE store and a point write there spreads all of it; the only timed writes there are the two-axis script's four moves. The churn and relation wirings, which subscribe after their rows are resolved, hold one store per row and copy that row alone. And a computed that loses its last listener is NOT detached from its sources inside this process: nanostores runs that teardown out of setTimeout(STORE_UNMOUNT_DELAY = 1000) (lifecycle/index.js) and no worker here yields to the event loop, so wherever a computed is involved — the wide, chain and diamond churn shapes, and the two window computeds of the cell row — an unmount splices a listener out and leaves the dependency edges standing. WHICH WAY THAT MOVES THESE NUMBERS IS NOT MEASURED: the unmount does less work, and every later write in the same sample notifies a computed nobody reads. Nothing here has priced either half. And in the read wiring a removal leaves the group index through one Set delete per id, where other rows splice or rebuild the group's array.

participants.name: redux-toolkit
participants.admission: the row values live in the Redux store — the rows slice's `entities` record, written only by its reducers — and `store.subscribe`, which Redux calls at the end of every dispatch, is what drives the consumer; under the window and read wirings the `idsByGroup` index beside it is slice state written by those same reducers and holds ids, never values.
participants.departure: no createEntityAdapter, the normalising guide's own helper: its upsert assigns a freshly built object per row, which defeats the Immer no-op the re-send scenario measures. Each subscriber applies react-redux useSelector's default bail-out — a view is delivered only when what it selected differs by reference from last time — which this bench drives without React; every selector returning an array is a reselect `createSelector` with `resultEqualityCheck: shallowEqual` (react-redux's), so a recomputed view holding the same row objects keeps its old reference, and each pinned cell compares its own selected string. Outside a frame every write is one action; inside `frame` the writes are buffered and dispatched as ONE `edited` action as the frame returns, the style guide's "avoid dispatching many actions in a row". churn.column selects the label string and compares it by `===`, exactly as the row shapes compare the selected row. A reducer rebuilds each touched group array once per action by filtering its original; the timed teardown is the two unsubscribe calls, leaving the store to the collector.

participants.name: preact-signals
participants.admission: every row is a @preact/signals-core signal per mutable field (group, rank, label, note), and the id and group maps beside them hold handles to those signals rather than any value; the change signal is preact's own effect, run when the outermost batch returns.
participants.departure: a removal of up to eight ids copies each touched bucket without that row, and a larger one rebuilds each touched bucket signal once for the whole batch rather than per removed row.

participants.name: alien-signals
participants.admission: every column lives in an alien-signals `signal` — a row is a signal per mutable field (group, rank, label, note), read by calling it — and each consumer is driven by alien's own `effect`, queued by the graph and run synchronously by `endBatch` or by the unbatched write itself. The id -> signal and group -> signal maps this adapter keeps hold handles only, never a value.
participants.departure: batched with startBatch()/endBatch(), which the cited README does not document — the pair was read out of the installed type declarations and implementation, because alien-signals ships no batch(fn) wrapper and un-batched writes would flush an effect per row. A bucket is mutated in place and announced with the documented trigger(); a removal of up to eight ids splices each out of its bucket, and a larger one compacts each touched bucket once for the whole batch rather than per removed row.

participants.name: zustand
participants.docs: https://github.com/pmndrs/zustand#readme — "Using subscribe with selector", "Using zustand without React"
participants.admission: the row values live in one vanilla zustand store — the `entities` record of its state, replaced only through `setState` — and the store's own listener set, run by `setState` before it returns and filtered by `subscribeWithSelector`, is what drives every consumer; under the window and read wirings the `idsByGroup` lists beside `entities` are state of the same store and hold ids, never values.
participants.departure: driven through the vanilla API with no React: every consumer is a `subscribeWithSelector` listener, the same selector-plus-equality a `useStore(store, selector)` hook re-renders on, and a selector returning a fresh array is compared with the shipped `shallow`, as `useShallow` does. zustand has no batch API: `setState` is its bulk update, so `frame` buffers the writes issued inside it and applies them as ONE `setState` as it returns, which copies `entities` once and notifies every listener once; outside a frame each write is its own `setState`. Writes are the documented immutable updates: a `setState` spreads the whole `entities` record, about ten thousand keys, to give the changed rows fresh references, and a re-send or a same-value patch produces fresh row objects and notifies, because nothing in the library compares values before notifying — the `immer` middleware, which would make a re-send a no-op the way Immer does in Redux Toolkit, is not used. Every selector re-runs on every `setState`, so a window view re-derives its group's top-k per `setState` and the cell and relation views rebuild their text arrays per `setState`. churn.chain and churn.diamond are derived with `reselect` `createSelector`, the memoised-selector pattern a zustand user writes for derived state: each level is a memoised selector over the level below, the subscriber is a `subscribeWithSelector` listener on the top one, and zustand itself ships no derivation. A group array is copied once per `setState` and each leaving id is spliced out of that copy.

participants.name: valtio
participants.admission: the row columns live in valtio proxies — one per row, filed under `rows` and, in the window and read wirings, under its group's bucket in `byGroup` of the same `proxy` state — and the change signal is valtio's own listener notification, run inside the write by `subscribe(…, true)` and `subscribeKey(…, true)`, which marks the view that `settle` renders.
participants.departure: driven through `valtio/vanilla` with no React. Every consumer is `subscribe(proxy, cb, true)` or `subscribeKey(proxy, key, cb, true)`: the default subscribe defers its callback to a microtask (vanilla.js:210-216) and no worker here yields, so the sync flag (vanilla.js:206-208) is the only arm that reaches a consumer at all. The callback only marks its view; `settle` renders the marked views, standing in for the microtask boundary at which the default subscribe would have coalesced the same notifications. valtio has no batch, so `frame` calls its function directly and every property set inside it runs the sync listeners of the proxy and of every listened-to ancestor. A subscription is to a WHOLE SUBTREE: a window view listens to its group bucket, so a note write or a write to a row below the window wakes it and delivers text it already shows, and the read wiring's view A listens to the cursor and to its group's bucket, re-subscribed on every switch. Every row object written is wrapped in its own Proxy on the way in (vanilla.js:63), and in the window and read wirings each row proxy sits in two parents, the population and its group bucket. A write of an existing row is `Object.assign` onto its proxy, so valtio's per-property `Object.is` (vanilla.js:56) makes a re-send of unchanged values notify nothing. The wide churn subscriber is one subscribe per source with one shared body, because subscribe takes one proxy. The chain and diamond shapes are declined: valtio 2.3.2 ships no derived value, and `derive-valtio` is not installed.

participants.name: xstate-store
participants.admission: the row values live in the context of an @xstate/store store — its `rows` record, replaced only by the store's own transitions — and the change signal is the store's atom, which `send` sets and which pushes through the `select`/`createAtom` computeds subscribed over it; under the window and read wirings the `idsByGroup` index beside the rows is context written by the same transitions and holds ids, never values.
participants.departure: @xstate/store 4.2.3 exports no batch or transaction (xstate-store.js:2, :90); its coalescing is `enqueue.trigger`, whose events run inside the SAME transition and commit with one `atom.set` (store-55b22bbd.js:847-875, :646-649). So `frame` buffers the row events issued inside it and sends ONE `framed` event whose handler re-triggers each of them through `enqueue.trigger`: a frame is one transition and one notification. Each triggered event is still its own handler, so a frame of k point writes spreads the rows record k times. Outside a frame each write is its own `send`. Events are sent as `store.send({ type, ... })` objects rather than through `store.trigger`, which the README calls equivalent and which spreads the payload into a fresh event object per call (store-55b22bbd.js:543-549, :590-598). Every window, cell, read and relation view passes the package's own exported `shallowEqual` (xstate-store.js:13-27) as the `select`/`createAtom` comparator — view A's paged atom compares its offset and then its rows with it — so a recomputed view whose rows are the same objects is not delivered; the row, column and single subscribers keep the default `Object.is`. The rows record is updated immutably by spread, the README's pattern (README.md:28-45), so a point event copies the whole population's record once. The read wiring keeps view A's cursor in a second store and the relation wiring keeps owners and pairs in a store each, beside the rows store. A removal splices each id out of its group bucket one row at a time.

participants.name: vue-reactivity
participants.admission: every row is a @vue/reactivity `shallowRef` per mutable field (group, rank, label, note), and the id and group maps beside them hold handles to those refs rather than any value; the change signal is the ref's own dep trigger, which queues each subscribed effect through its `scheduler` for `settle` to run.
participants.departure: @vue/reactivity 3.5.43 exports no batch — startBatch/endBatch exist in the build but are not exported — so every `effect` is created with the `scheduler` option its declarations (`ReactiveEffectOptions.scheduler`) expose: a trigger only queues the effect, and `settle` runs each queued effect whose `dirty` is set, which is the queue @vue/runtime-core's scheduler keeps and this package does not ship. `frame` therefore calls its function directly. A bucket is mutated in place and announced with the documented `triggerRef`; a removal of up to eight ids splices each out of its bucket, and a larger one compacts each touched bucket once for the whole call rather than per removed row.

participants.name: solid-js
participants.admission: every row is a solid-js `createSignal` per mutable field (group, rank, label, note), and the id and group maps beside them hold the [get, set] pairs of those signals rather than any value; the change signal is solid's own `createEffect`, run when the outermost update returns.
participants.departure: the reactive core is imported as `solid-js/dist/solid.js` and not as `solid-js`: the worker runs under node without the "browser" condition, where `solid-js` resolves to dist/server.js, whose createEffect is an empty function and whose signals track nothing. `solid-js/store` is not used for the same reason: store/dist/store.js imports the bare `solid-js` (line 1), so under node its proxies would read the server build's untracked signals. A bucket signal is created with `equals: false`, mutated in place and set to the same array to notify; a removal of up to eight ids splices each out of its bucket, and a larger one compacts each touched bucket once for the whole batch rather than per removed row.

participants.name: tanstack-store
participants.admission: every row's columns live in a @tanstack/store `createAtom` holder whose compare always reports a change, so a write mutates the held row in place and sets the same reference back; the id and group maps beside them hold handles to those atoms rather than any value; the change signal is the library's own `subscribe` on a derived atom, run when the outermost `batch` returns.
participants.departure: a removal compacts each touched bucket array once, in place, for the whole batch rather than per removed row, so a batch of removals out of one group is one pass over it and not one per id.

excluded.name: tanstack-table
excluded.reason: a headless view layer: it never holds the rows (`data` stays the caller's array) and has no change signal for them — `onStateChange` reports table state, never data. Neither half of the rule, so there is no store here to compare.

scenarios.label: batch insert
scenarios.description: One step: every row is inserted into an empty store in one batch. Both views go from empty to a full page and must each re-render exactly once.

scenarios.label: insert into a populated store
scenarios.description: One step: 100 new rows are inserted in one batch into a full store, with every group sorted and every visible row subscribed. They sort first, so they appear at the top of every group and both views must change. "batch insert" fills an empty store; this adds to one already in use.

scenarios.label: the population keeps growing
scenarios.description: 8 steps. Each inserts a batch of new rows spread over every group and sorted first, and nothing is deleted, so the store ends forty per cent larger than it started. A store grown step by step is not the same as one loaded in one go: sorted lists and indexes can cost more as they grow. Every batch shows at the top of both views.

scenarios.label: cold start to first render
scenarios.description: One step, timed from nothing: create the store and both views, subscribe them, insert every row, and render the first page of each view. The only scenario that times creating the store. Compare with "batch insert", the same work without creating the store: the difference is what setting up a store and its subscriptions costs.

scenarios.label: tear the screen down
scenarios.description: One step: the whole screen, a full store with both views and every subscription, is disposed. The teardown itself must render nothing. Afterwards, outside the timing, rows are written into the disposed screen and nothing may render, so a dispose that disposed nothing fails instead of looking fastest. A library that refuses that write also passes.

scenarios.label: teardown lower bound
scenarios.description: Lower bound, no library: a hand-written screen (every row in a Map, two views and one subscriber per visible row) is discarded by dropping the single reference to it. No library can tear a screen down for less. Afterwards, outside the timing, rows are written into the discarded screen and nothing may render.

scenarios.label: patch one column
scenarios.description: 32 steps. Each step changes the `label` of one row visible in view A. View A must re-render with the new text every step. View B shows a different group and must not change; how often it was woken anyway is counted.

scenarios.label: patch a row off screen
scenarios.description: 32 steps. Each step changes the `label` of a row in view A's group that sits just below the visible page: in the group, but not on screen. Neither view may re-render. Measured: how often a library wakes a view for a change nobody can see.

scenarios.label: patch an unread column
scenarios.description: 32 steps. The same rows and the same calls as "patch one column", but the changed field is `note`, which no view displays. Neither view may re-render. The difference between the two scenarios is what tracking changes per field saves.

scenarios.label: batch patch
scenarios.description: One step: the `label` of every tenth row in the whole store (at least four pages of rows, spread over every group) is changed inside one batch, and the changes are delivered once. This is a sync response or a bulk edit. Most changes land in groups no view shows. Both views must end showing the new text. How many times each re-renders is up to the library: one with a batch API renders once per view, one without renders once per changed visible row, so only the final screen is checked.

scenarios.label: batch patch an unread column
scenarios.description: One step: the same rows as "batch patch" are changed in one batch, but in `note`, a field no view displays. Neither view may show new text; any re-render is wasted work and is counted. Against "batch patch" it shows the cost of a batch nobody sees; against "patch an unread column" it shows what batching saves. The changes are checked in the store afterwards.

scenarios.label: most rows change every frame
scenarios.description: 2 steps. Each step changes the `label` of one row in 2 across the whole store, the same share of every group, and delivers once. Every other write scenario changes a handful of rows; this one checks the opposite end, where most of what is subscribed changes at once. Both views must end every step showing new text.

scenarios.label: one frame, every kind of change
scenarios.description: One step with five kinds of change delivered together: 4 new rows inserted at the top of view A, its last 4 rows deleted, `label` changed on rows in between, 4 rows moved to group B, and a few rows re-sorted inside view A. Each kind touches different rows. This is what one message from a server can carry; every other scenario has one kind. Both views must end full and correct, with a new row at the top of view A.

scenarios.label: row moves between groups
scenarios.description: 8 steps. Each step moves one row from group A to group B or back. The moved rows sort first, so every move shows at the top of both views: view A loses a row and pulls in the next one from below, view B gains it.

scenarios.label: a row arrives mid-order
scenarios.description: 4 steps. Each step changes one row's `group` and `rank` together, so it leaves the top of view A and lands in the middle of view B, not at its top. Compare with "row moves between groups", where the row always lands at position 0, the cheapest place to insert into a sorted list. Both views must change every step and stay full, and the final positions are checked.

scenarios.label: sort key moves
scenarios.description: 8 steps. Each step changes one row's `rank` so that it moves to another place inside view A. The same rows stay on screen; only their order changes. View B must not change.

scenarios.label: the whole window re-sorted
scenarios.description: 8 steps. Each step changes the `rank` of all 32 rows of view A at once, so the whole page is reordered while the same rows stay on it. Compare with "sort key moves", which moves one row: together they show how the cost of keeping a list sorted grows with how much of the order changed. View B must not change.

scenarios.label: a consumer per group
scenarios.description: 50 steps, with one view per group (50 views) instead of two. Each step reorders rows inside one group's page, so exactly one view may re-render. Measured: how many of the other 49 views were woken anyway. A library that notifies only the affected group wakes 50 views in total; one that notifies everybody wakes 50 × 50, and each of those views re-renders its page.

scenarios.label: targeted column delivery
scenarios.description: 16 steps over 8 rows that are looked up once before timing starts. View A shows their `label`, view B their `note`. The first half of the steps changes each `label`, the second half each `note`. A change must reach only the view showing that field: a library that tracks fields wakes one view per change, one that tracks whole rows wakes both, and one that tracks nothing re-reads everything.

scenarios.label: cell lower bound
scenarios.description: Lower bound, no library: the steps of "targeted column delivery", each rendering one changed line of a 8-line view straight from an array of strings. A library that notifies only the view showing the changed field renders this much; one that notifies both views renders twice as much.

scenarios.label: delete the visible window
scenarios.description: One step: all 32 rows view A shows, the top of group A, are deleted in one batch. View A must re-render once, refilled with the rows that were below it. View B shows a different group and must not change.

scenarios.label: delete one visible row
scenarios.description: 8 steps. Each step deletes one row view A shows, from different positions on the page: js-framework-benchmark's "remove row". View A must re-render once per step and stay full, pulling up the next row from below. View B must not change. Compare with "delete the visible window", which deletes the whole page at once.

scenarios.label: the group empties under the view
scenarios.description: Two steps, starting with group A empty. Step one inserts every row of group A, so its list is built from nothing; step two deletes all of them in one batch, so view A must end showing an empty list. No other scenario empties a list. Afterwards the store is checked for rows a partial delete left behind. View B shows a different group and must not change.

scenarios.label: re-send unchanged list
scenarios.description: One step: the 32 rows view A shows are written again, as new objects, with exactly the values they already have, like a page fetched again from a server. The benchmark code does not filter them out, so this shows whether the library itself notices that nothing changed. No view may show new text; how often views were woken for nothing is counted.

scenarios.label: consumer lower bound
scenarios.description: Lower bound, no library: a page of 32 rows rendered 32 times straight from an array of plain objects. Every participant renders through the same code, so no library can render a page for less; one that stores rows as proxies or wrapped objects also pays to read through them.

scenarios.label: mount lower bound
scenarios.description: Lower bound, no library: 8 cycles of subscribing 256 callbacks to one plain object, changing it, running them, unsubscribing all, changing it again. Subscribers live in a plain array with constant-time removal. No library can subscribe and unsubscribe for less; the mount and unmount tables are scaled by it.

scenarios.label: mount and unmount one subscriber
scenarios.description: 8 cycles of: subscribe one component to one row, change the row; unsubscribe, change it again. The smallest mount and unmount, which every other mount and unmount scenario is compared with. The first change must reach the component once; the second must reach nobody.

scenarios.label: N subscribers on one root, oldest out first
scenarios.description: 8 cycles of: subscribe 32 components to the same row, change it, unsubscribe them oldest first, change it again. This is a list of components bound to one shared object being mounted and unmounted. Compare with "mount and unmount one subscriber" for the cost per component, and with the N×8 variant for whether that cost grows with the number already subscribed.

scenarios.label: N subscribers on one root, newest out first
scenarios.description: The same as "N subscribers on one root, oldest out first", but the 32 components unsubscribe newest first. The difference shows whether the order of unmounting matters: a library that keeps subscribers in an array pays differently for removing from its front and from its back.

scenarios.label: N×8 subscribers on one root, oldest out first
scenarios.description: The same as "N subscribers on one root, oldest out first" with 256 components instead of 32. If unsubscribing is linear, eight times the components cost eight times more; sixty-four times more means it is quadratic. One size cannot tell those apart, which is why there are two.

scenarios.label: N×8 subscribers on one root, newest out first
scenarios.description: 256 components on one row, unsubscribing newest first. With the other three variants it shows whether the effect of unmount order grows with the number of components or stays constant.

scenarios.label: one subscriber over many sources
scenarios.description: 8 cycles of: subscribe one component that reads 64 rows, change the first of them, unsubscribe, change it again. The other variants vary how many components watch one row; this one varies how many rows one component watches, which is what a subscription pays to register with each of its sources and to leave them. Compare with "mount and unmount one subscriber", whose component reads one row.

scenarios.label: N subscribers on one column
scenarios.description: The same as "N subscribers on one root, oldest out first" (32 components, 8 cycles), but each component subscribes to one field of the row, `label`, instead of the whole row. The difference is what subscribing to a single field costs. A library with no per-field subscription skips this scenario rather than repeat its whole-row number.

scenarios.label: N subscribers on N rows, a list
scenarios.description: 8 cycles of: subscribe 32 components, each to its own row, the way a list mounts one component per row; change some of those rows in one batch; unsubscribe them oldest first; change the same rows again. Each cycle changes 4 fewer rows, so the number of components that re-render proves each watches its own row. After unsubscribing nobody may be notified. Compare with "N subscribers on one root, oldest out first", where all components share one row.

scenarios.label: N subscribers over a derivation chain
scenarios.description: A dashboard of 32 tiles; tile i summarises rows i to i+7 through a chain of 4 derived values, built when the tile mounts, like a component's selectors. 8 cycles of: mount all tiles, change row 0, unmount them oldest first, change row 0 again. Only tile 0 reads row 0, so exactly one tile may update, and after unmounting none may. Measured: building chains of derived values on mount and taking them apart on unmount.

scenarios.label: a write through standing chains
scenarios.description: The same 32-tile dashboard as "N subscribers over a derivation chain", mounted before timing starts. 16 steps, each changing row 7: the 8 tiles that read it must recompute their chains and the rest must not wake. Nothing is mounted or unmounted, so this is the cost of running the chains; the other scenario is the cost of building them.

scenarios.label: N subscribers over a diamond
scenarios.description: 8 cycles of: mount 32 components, each building its own diamond, two values derived from row 0 and a third that combines both; change row 0; unmount them oldest first; change it again. The combined value must be computed once per change, not once per branch: computing it twice is the "glitch" this checks for. Compare with "N subscribers over a derivation chain", where the derived values form a line.

scenarios.label: a write through standing diamonds
scenarios.description: The same 32 diamonds as "N subscribers over a diamond", mounted before timing starts. 16 steps, each changing row 0: every diamond recomputes once per step. Nothing is mounted or unmounted, so this is the cost of running diamonds; the other scenario is the cost of building them.

scenarios.label: churn against a standing population
scenarios.description: 256 components stay subscribed to one row the whole time. 8 cycles of: subscribe 32 more to the same row, change it, unsubscribe those, change it again. A real screen keeps most of its subscriptions and mounts or unmounts a few; this shows whether that costs more when many subscribers are already there.

scenarios.label: an application screen fills
scenarios.description: An app screen: 80 cards in 10 decks owned by 5 users, already in the store. In one step, 180 components mount (one per card, one per tag shown on a card, one per deck name, and one per deck date, which reads a setting of the deck's user) and 46 of the 95 records change. The only scenario where data changes and components mount together. Exactly 87 components, those whose own record changed, must re-render.

scenarios.label: an application screen in use
scenarios.description: The same app screen as "an application screen fills", mounted before timing starts. 20 rounds, each one step: every card's tag list grows by one tag, or drops from 4 back to one, mounting or unmounting tag components; every deck is renamed, every card toggled, and one user's setting changed. Mounts, unmounts and changes to cards, decks and users happen together. Each round must produce one update with exactly the expected components re-rendered.

scenarios.label: one setting moves
scenarios.description: The same app screen as "an application screen fills", mounted before timing starts. 20 steps, each changing one user's setting. Only that user's 2 deck-date components read it and must update; nothing else may. Measured: how quickly a library finds the few components that depend on a value stored in another record.

scenarios.label: read a page by key
scenarios.description: 8 steps. Each looks up 32 rows by key, spread across the whole store, and renders `id rank label` for each. Nothing is written: the only scenario that times reading rather than reacting to a change. The keys may not be looked up in advance. The hand-written baseline answers with one Map lookup per key.

scenarios.label: scroll the window
scenarios.description: 8 steps. Each scrolls view A within group A, a quarter page at a time down to one full page and back to the top. No data changes. Every step must show a new page; view B, a filtered view of the same group that does not scroll, must not change. Compare with "the whole window re-sorted": there the data moves under a fixed page, here the page moves over fixed data.

scenarios.label: scroll deep into the group
scenarios.description: 8 steps. Like "scroll the window", but view A jumps in four equal steps to the last full page of the group and back, as in virtual scrolling far from the top. No data changes. A library that keeps the group sorted jumps straight to the position; one that does not sorts the whole group again and discards everything above the page. Every step must show a full new page; view B must not change.

scenarios.label: the view switches group
scenarios.description: 8 steps. Each switches view A to another group, like a user changing tab or filter: 7 different groups, then back to group A. No data changes. Every step must show a full page of the new group from its top; view B must not change. A library that keeps a list per group reads another list; one that does not filters the whole store again.

scenarios.label: a view filtered on two axes
scenarios.description: 4 steps with two views of the same group: view A filters by `group` only, view B by `group` and a second condition. The steps move two rows out of the group and back: one that matches view B's second condition and one that does not. View A must update all four times, view B only twice. Measured: how often view B was woken for a row its filter already excluded.

scenarios.label: relation lower bound
scenarios.description: Lower bound, no library: the 16 steps of "a write to a related entity" and "a record keyed by two identities", each rendering the changed view straight from arrays of strings. Looking up the linked records is left out, because that is what those two scenarios measure. No library can come out below it.

scenarios.label: a write to a related entity
scenarios.description: 8 steps with two record types: 8 rows each point to an owner, 4 owners with two rows each. Each step changes one owner's `name`; no row changes. View A shows each row with its owner's name, so it must update and two of its lines change. View B shows the same rows through another linked record and must not change. No row changes its owner.

scenarios.label: a record keyed by two identities
scenarios.description: 8 steps. Each changes the `mark` of a record identified by a pair (owner, row), with the two-part key built fresh on every call. View B shows these marks and must update every step; view A must not change. Measured: finding a record by a two-part key; a hand-written store joins the two ids into a string and looks it up in a Map. The records exist before timing starts, so nothing is created.

scenarios.label: single-value lower bound
scenarios.description: Lower bound, no library: 32 renders of one line, each with a different value, with no store. Every single-value scenario renders through the same code, so the gap between a library and this bound is the library's own cost.

scenarios.label: write one value
scenarios.description: 32 steps. Each sets a new value on one standalone value: no key, no collection, no list. View A shows it and must update every step. A second value beside it never changes and must not update; how often its view was woken anyway is counted.

scenarios.label: re-write one value
scenarios.description: 32 steps. Each sets one standalone value to the value it already has. The benchmark code does not filter this out, so it shows whether the library compares before it notifies: if it does, nothing renders; if not, the same line renders every step.

LokiJS HAS NO COLUMN IDENTITY. `update` is document-level: the event carries the document, and with cloning off the "old" document it also carries is THE SAME OBJECT, so nothing in the library can say which column moved. Telling them apart needs either a cloned collection with the adapter comparing old and new labels, or the adapter remembering the last label, and both are the adapter doing the library's job, which the B3 clause of churnColumn forbids. The row and wide shapes are supplied and unaffected.

LokiJS HAS NO DERIVED VALUE A SECOND DERIVATION CAN READ. A DynamicView is a filtered, sorted list over one collection and cannot take another view as its source, and the collection emitter has no per-source channel, so a mount would be the wide shape's collection listener with the depth levels re-run by hand inside its body, which the B3 clause of churnChain forbids: the adapter building the chain, not the library, and the wide shape's row printed under the chain's name.
